article_title: Better P-curves: Making P-curve analysis more robust to errors, fraud, and ambitious P-hacking, a Reply to Ulrich and Miller (2015).
citation: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2015). Better P-Curves: Making P-Curve Analysis More Robust To Errors, Fraud, and Ambitious P-Hacking, A Reply To Ulrich and Miller (2015). Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), 1146–1152. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000104
title: P-curve analysis: the distribution of significant p values diagnoses evidential value, null results, and p-hacking
description: P-curve analysis is a tool for assessing whether a set of statistically significant findings contains evidential value. It examines the distribution of significant p values: "True effects, those that differ from zero, lead to right-skewed p-curves (e.g., more .01s than .04s). Nonexistent effects lead to flat p-curves". Many forms of p-hacking lead to left-skewed p-curves, so a right-skewed observed p-curve rules out selective reporting of significant results as the sole explanation.
requirements: Included p values must test the hypothesis of interest, have a uniform distribution under the null, and be statistically independent of other p values
constraints: The framework assumes that among significant results, the magnitude of the p value does not affect whether it gets reported
target_learners: researchers conducting or evaluating p-curve analyses
target_learning_goals: assessing whether a set of published studies contains evidential value
examples: The authors applied p-curve to a set of JPSP experiments reported only with a covariate, observing a significantly left-skewed p-curve
key_sources: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2015). Better P-Curves: Making P-Curve Analysis More Robust To Errors, Fraud, and Ambitious P-Hacking, A Reply To Ulrich and Miller (2015). Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), 1146–1152. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000104

article_title: Better performance of medical students on pharmacotherapy knowledge and skills tests is associated with practising with e-learning program P-scribe.
citation: Kalfsvel L, Versmissen J, van Doorn A, van den Broek W, van der Kuy H, van Rosse F. (2022). Better performance of medical students on pharmacotherapy knowledge and skills tests is associated with practising with e‐learning program P‐scribe. Br J Clin Pharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.15077
title: P-scribe e-learning platform for pharmacotherapy education
description: P-scribe is a Dutch web-based e-learning platform for pharmacy and medical students, used at all Dutch university medical centres and several Belgian medical centres. E-learning modules can be built adapted to curriculum needs and are based around the WHO 6-step model for rational pharmacotherapy. Students are "guided through different life‐like cases in which a change in pharmacotherapy is needed", each module focusing on a different aspect such as side-effects or polypharmacy. At Erasmus MC it is used in the medical master's curriculum as part of flipped classroom teaching.
requirements: Modules are developed by medical doctors and pharmacists working as clinical pharmacotherapy teachers
Students have personal accounts with data tracking enabled
constraints: Data tracking records the time the module was open on the computer, not how much time the student actually spent on it
examples: At Erasmus MC, e-learning modules are used in the master's curriculum as part of flipped classroom teaching, with compulsory and non-compulsory modules embedded throughout
key_sources: Kalfsvel L, Versmissen J, van Doorn A, van den Broek W, van der Kuy H, van Rosse F. (2022). Better performance of medical students on pharmacotherapy knowledge and skills tests is associated with practising with e‐learning program P‐scribe. Br J Clin Pharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.15077

article_title: The Flight Physics Concept Inventory: Development of a research-based assessment instrument to enhance learning and teaching
citation: Florian Genz. (2025). The Flight Physics Concept Inventory: Development of a research-based assessment instrument to enhance learning and teaching. Springer Spektrum. http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-47515-4
title: Knowledge-in-pieces framing of concepts: p-prims and resources as building blocks of concepts
description: The thesis adopts diSessa's and Hammer's knowledge-in-pieces account as its working theory of concepts. P-prims are ideas that cannot be learned explicitly and are neither correct nor incorrect in themselves; they can only be applied (in)appropriately in a given context. The author defines a concept as "the higher level-thinking structure emerging from the use and application of p-prims/resources in a given context", with naive concepts defined as ideas inconsistent with expert ideas.
requirements: Instruction should attend to students' prior ideas rather than dismiss variations as noise
constraints: The judgmental terms naive concept and misconcept carry a judgment of lesser applicability, so avoiding them when communicating to students can be advantageous at first
target_learning_goals: conceptual change from naive to expert-like concepts
examples: The thesis contrasts this with the 1980s conceptual change model of Posner and colleagues, which diSessa and colleagues challenged and refined in the 1990s.
key_sources: Florian Genz. (2025). The Flight Physics Concept Inventory: Development of a research-based assessment instrument to enhance learning and teaching. Springer Spektrum. http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-658-47515-4

article_title: Dissecting Physics Reasoning in Small Language Models: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis from an Educational Perspective
citation: Nicy Scaria, Silvester John Joseph Kennedy, Krishna Agarwal, Diksha Seth, Deepak Subramani. (2025). Dissecting Physics Reasoning in Small Language Models: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis from an Educational Perspective. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20707
title: P-REFS: a stage-wise rubric for evaluating physics reasoning step by step
description: P-REFS (Physics Reasoning Evaluation Framework for Step-by-step Analysis) is a 10-point rubric that scores SLM physics solutions at distinct reasoning stages rather than by final answer alone. The article describes it as "a 10-point framework evaluating three components: Problem Formulation (0-2 pts) for interpretation and modeling, Step-by-step Solution (0-6 pts) encompassing conceptual planning, execution accuracy, and logical progression, and Final Answer (0-2 pts)". It was operationalized via an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline, with Gemini 2.5 Flash selected after expert validation against two independent physics-graduate reviewers on 550 question-response pairs per candidate judge.
requirements: An LLM judge with specialized prompts per question type, validated against expert human grading
Structured or adaptable response formats so steps can be scored independently
constraints: The LLM-as-a-judge framework may introduce systematic bias on numerical precision, unit conversions, and algebraic equivalence
Judge validation was conducted on a limited subset and may not reflect behavior across the full benchmark
target_learning_goals: diagnosing stage-wise reasoning failures in physics problem solving
examples: Errors were categorized into eight types: Interpretation, Modeling, Conceptual, Concept Application, Calculation, Correctness, Coherence, and Final Answer
key_sources: Nicy Scaria, Silvester John Joseph Kennedy, Krishna Agarwal, Diksha Seth, Deepak Subramani. (2025). Dissecting Physics Reasoning in Small Language Models: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis from an Educational Perspective. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20707

article_title: General students' misconceptions related to Electricity and Magnetism
citation: Cristian Raduta. (2000). General Students' Misconceptions Related to Electricity and Magnetism. The Ohio State University. https://www.physics.ohio-state.edu/~aubrecht/OSmisE&M.html
title: P-prims (phenomenological primitives) as an explanatory framework for persistent E&M misconceptions
description: P-prims, or "phenomenological primitives" (diSessa), are "relatively minimal abstractions of simple common phenomena"—explanations students use to explain everyday phenomena before learning any physics. Physics-naive students hold a large collection of p-prims and appeal to them as self-contained explanations; during physics learning some cease being primitives. The review applies this framework to E&M misconceptions such as treating the N pole as positively charged ("opposites attract and likes repel each other") and "more implies more, or bigger cause implies bigger effect," arguing these intuitions are so strongly rooted that they survive instruction.
requirements: Instructors should know the repertoire of p-prims related to E&M that naive students hold, so analogies can be built on them when teaching advanced concepts
constraints: The review frames p-prim explanations as a possible account, not a tested result; the suggested misconception areas it connects to p-prims are partly the author's own speculations
target_learning_goals: understanding of electric and magnetic fields
overcoming persistent misconceptions about magnetism and electromagnetism
examples: Maloney's finding that most students treated the N pole as positively charged before and after instruction is read as a strongly rooted p-prim; Galili's double-pendulum results are read as the 'bigger cause implies bigger effect' p-prim overriding Newton's third law
key_sources: Cristian Raduta. (2000). General Students' Misconceptions Related to Electricity and Magnetism. The Ohio State University. https://www.physics.ohio-state.edu/~aubrecht/OSmisE&M.html
